summary: A volcanic island nation in the Windward Islands of the eastern Caribbean. It changed hands between Britain and France 14 times, became independent from Britain in 1979, and is known for the Pitons.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 17th and 18th centuries, French colonists established sugar plantations on Saint Lucia and required enslaved people to be baptized as Catholics. After Britain gained Saint Lucia in 1814, Catholicism remained the faith of the great majority of islanders, and the Church long dominated education and social life. Today Catholic festivals and Masses are still important cultural events on the island.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Seventh-day Adventist, Pentecostal, Anglican, etc.)
ranking.description: Anglicanism was introduced after British rule began in 1814, but it had a limited following. In the mid to late 20th century, Seventh-day Adventist, Pentecostal and Baptist churches arrived from the United States and other Caribbean islands, attracting followers with lively worship, radio broadcasting and community services, so that the various Protestant denominations have continued to grow in recent decades.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The proportion of people with no religion in Saint Lucia is gradually rising, mainly among young people in urban areas such as the capital Castries. It is linked to globalization, the spread of education, and doubts about the authority of traditional churches.

ranking.name: Rastafari
ranking.description: Rastafari originated in Jamaica in the 1930s. In the 1970s, through the influence of reggae music and Bob Marley, it spread to Saint Lucia and other eastern Caribbean islands, attracting young people with its anti-colonial ideas and its emphasis on African identity. Early adherents came into conflict with the government and society over practices such as smoking cannabis.

religion.background: The indigenous Kalinago (Carib) people resisted European colonization for over a century. From 1660 France and Britain fought over Saint Lucia as many as fourteen times. French colonial rule (mainly in the 17th and 18th centuries) brought Catholicism, and a Catholic society was built around French planters and enslaved people brought from West Africa. Britain formally acquired Saint Lucia in 1814 but did not force the islanders to change their religion, so Catholicism continued as the majority faith. From the 20th century, Protestant denominations such as the Seventh-day Adventists and Pentecostals arrived from the United States and other Caribbean countries, and Saint Lucia became independent in 1979.

ranking.name: Saint Lucian Creole French (Kwéyòl)
ranking.description: Kwéyòl originated during the French colonial period of the 17th and 18th centuries, when enslaved people combined French-based vocabulary with West African languages. Although Britain promoted English after taking over in 1814, Creole remained the mother tongue of many Saint Lucians at home and in the countryside. After independence in 1979, social attitudes toward Kwéyòl changed and the government came to support Creole cultural festivals, but it is still not widely used in schools or on official occasions.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the official language after Britain acquired Saint Lucia in 1814, and it is used in schools, government, courts and the media. Since the 20th century, English education has become widespread, and more and more urban young people use English as their main language, so English and Creole are used side by side.

language.history: In the 17th and 18th centuries Saint Lucia was colonized mainly by France. Enslaved people brought from West Africa came into contact with French planters and developed a Creole language (Kwéyòl) based on French vocabulary and combined with West African grammar. After Britain acquired Saint Lucia in 1814, English became the official language and was promoted in schools, while Creole was long forbidden in schools. After independence in 1979, Creole gradually gained recognition; each October the island holds Creole Day (Jounen Kwéyòl) to celebrate the culture, and some media and religious activities also use Creole.

ranking.name: Green fig and saltfish
ranking.description: Green bananas (called green figs locally) are boiled and served with salted cod sautéed with onion, tomato and sweet pepper. It is the national dish of Saint Lucia.
ranking.history: Salted cod was a product of colonial-era Atlantic trade: Canada and New England in North America exchanged salted cod for Caribbean sugar and rum, using it as a cheap source of protein for enslaved people. Bananas became Saint Lucia's main export crop in the 20th century, and unripe green bananas were treated as a starchy staple. The combination of the two reflects the history of the colonial plantation economy, and today it is a common dish at family breakfasts and Sunday tables.

ranking.name: Callaloo soup
ranking.description: A thick green soup stewed from dasheen (taro) leaves or amaranth leaves with coconut milk, onion, spices and salted meat. It has a smooth texture and the aroma of coconut milk and spices.
ranking.history: Callaloo originated as a West African leafy-vegetable stew. After enslaved people were brought to the Caribbean, local taro leaves or amaranth replaced the green leafy vegetables of Africa. On Saint Lucia and other eastern Caribbean islands, callaloo is a traditional Sunday lunch dish and also often appears at cultural festivals such as Creole Day, and it is regarded as one of the representative dishes of Afro-Caribbean culture.

ranking.name: Roti wrap
ranking.description: A thin flatbread made from wheat flour, wrapped around fillings such as curry chicken, curry goat, or potato and chickpeas. The bread is soft and the filling is fragrant and spicy, making it a convenient takeaway lunch.
ranking.history: Roti originated in India. After the abolition of slavery in 1838, Britain recruited indentured laborers from India to the Caribbean, and from 1859 Indian laborers were also brought to Saint Lucia's sugar plantations, bringing Indian flatbreads and curry dishes. These foods gradually blended into the local diet, and roti became a common lunch at street stalls and snack shops in Saint Lucia, reflecting the contribution of Indo-Caribbean people to local culture.

ranking.name: Cocoa tea
ranking.description: A hot drink made by simmering ground local cocoa with milk, cinnamon, nutmeg and bay leaves. It tastes rich and sweet, with the warmth of spices.
ranking.history: Cocoa is native to Central and South America. In the 18th century French colonists established cocoa plantations on Saint Lucia, and cocoa was for a time an important export crop. Islanders dry and roast cocoa beans at home and roll them into cocoa sticks, which are used to brew cocoa tea. Today cocoa tea is often drunk at breakfast or on cold rainy-season mornings, and cocoa cultivation in Saint Lucia is also being revived.

ranking.name: Accra (fried saltfish fritters)
ranking.description: Small fritters made by mixing soaked and flaked salted cod with batter, scallions, herbs and chili, then deep-frying. They are crispy outside and soft inside, with the savory taste of saltfish and chili.
ranking.history: Accra shares its name with Accra, the capital of Ghana in West Africa. It is generally thought to derive from the bean fritters (akara) of the Yoruba and other West African peoples; enslaved people brought the method to the Caribbean and adapted it to use salted cod, the main colonial-era ingredient. It is especially popular in the French-speaking Caribbean (Guadeloupe, Martinique and Saint Lucia) and is a street snack and festival treat.
